answer:
A whole-fund conversion generally turns existing mutual-fund shares into ETF shares; it doesn’t leave investors choosing between share classes.

Check the fund’s official notices and prospectus supplement for the effective date, any election or account-update deadlines, and what happens if you do nothing. Procedures vary. Direct holders may need to open or update an ETF-capable brokerage account, provide tax or identity information, or make transfer or registration changes. Confirm whether the fund or transfer agent will move shares automatically or needs your instructions.

After conversion, ETF shares trade through a brokerage during market hours, and direct mutual-fund purchase or redemption services may end. Check how fractional shares will be handled—they may be paid out in cash, sold, or treated another way. Don’t assume deadlines, trading availability, or fractional-share treatment; verify them in the fund’s notice.
original_answer:
A whole-fund conversion is different from adding an ETF share class: the existing mutual-fund shares generally convert into ETF shares, rather than leaving investors with a choice between classes.

Check the fund’s official notices and prospectus supplement for its effective date, any election or account-update deadlines, and what happens if you do nothing. Procedures vary. A direct holder may need to open or update a brokerage account that can hold and trade ETFs, provide required tax or identity information, and arrange any transfer or registration changes the fund requests. Confirm whether the fund or its transfer agent will move the shares automatically or require instructions.

After conversion, ETF shares trade through a brokerage during market hours; direct mutual-fund purchase/redemption services may end. Ask how fractional shares will be handled: they may be paid out in cash, sold, or treated another way under the fund’s terms. Don’t assume a deadline, trading availability, or fractional-share treatment without checking the notice.
